notes.text: For more than 8, cook the potatoes in three batches instead of two, so the pan isn't crowded.

callback.body: In your heat-control lesson you watched the pan and turned the heat up or down when the food told you to. Hash browns need that same eye, for the opposite job: hot enough to brown, but not so hot the outside burns before the middle cooks.

move.title: Dry potatoes, hot pan, hands off
move.body: Crisping means getting food brown and crunchy on the outside. Today you'll grate potatoes, rinse them, squeeze out every drop of water you can, and fry them in a hot pan without stirring, until they turn into a golden, crispy cake.

why.title: Water is the enemy of crisp
why.body: Wet potatoes in a pan make steam. Water can't get hotter than boiling, so while there's water, the potatoes steam and stay pale and soft. Squeeze out the water first, and the pan can get the potatoes hot enough to brown and crunch.

why.title: Rinse off the extra starch
why.body: Grating breaks open the potato and lets out loose starch and juice. Left on, it turns the shreds gummy, and it turns gray or pink in the air. A rinse in cold water washes it away, so the shreds stay separate and crisp.

why.title: Start with hot fat
why.body: If the fat is cold when the potatoes go in, they soak it up and turn greasy. Hot fat that shimmers seals the outside of each shred right away, so it fries instead of soaking.

why.title: Leave it alone
why.body: A brown crust only forms while the potatoes sit still against the hot pan. Every stir lifts them away from the heat and starts the clock over. When the crust is ready, it lets go of the pan on its own.

wrong.fix: There was too much water, or the pan was crowded. Squeeze the next batch harder, and make sure the fat shimmers before the potatoes go in.

wrong.sign: Dark outside, raw in the middle
wrong.fix: The heat was too high. Turn it down a notch, cover the pan for 2 minutes to cook the middle, then uncover so it crisps again.
That's just air on the cut potato. They still taste fine. Next time, get them into the water as you grate.

wrong.sign: It sticks when you try to flip it
wrong.fix: Wait another minute. When the crust is ready it lets go on its own. Add a little oil around the edges if the pan looks dry.

quiz.q: Why do you squeeze the shredded potatoes in a towel?
choices: Water makes steam, and steam keeps them soft
So they cook faster in the middle
quiz.explain: While there's water, the potatoes steam. Dry potatoes can get hot enough to brown.

quiz.q: The hash browns have been in the pan two minutes. Should you stir them?
choices: No, leave them alone so a crust forms
Yes, and press them with a fork
quiz.explain: The crust only forms while the potatoes sit still against the hot pan.

substitutions.note: Use 1 more tablespoon of oil in the pan for each batch.

steps.text: Rinse the potatoes and peel them.
steps.tip: Peel away from your hand, and keep your fingers behind the blade.

steps.text: Fill the large bowl about halfway with cold water.
Grate the potatoes on the large holes of the box grater. Every so often, scrape the shreds into the bowl of water.
steps.tip: Stop when a piece gets too small to hold with your fingers flat and away from the holes. Toss the little end in the water whole.

steps.text: Swish the shreds around in the water with your hand. Pour them into the colander and rinse with cold water until it runs clear, not cloudy.
Pile half the shreds in the middle of a clean kitchen towel. Gather up the corners, twist, and squeeze over the sink as hard as you can, until hardly any water drips. Do the same with the other half.
steps.tip: Squeeze more than you think you need to. Then once more.

steps.text: Dry the large bowl. Put the squeezed potatoes in it and toss with {qty:salt} salt and the pepper, pulling apart any clumps.
Put 2 tablespoons of oil and 1 tablespoon of butter in the skillet over medium heat. Wait until the butter stops foaming and the oil shimmers.
Scatter half the potatoes over the pan in an even layer, about ½ inch thick. Press them down flat with the spatula. Now leave them alone.
steps.tip: Lay them in close to the pan and away from you, so the oil doesn't splash toward you.

steps.text: Cook without stirring until the bottom is deep golden brown.
steps.look: Golden-brown edges, and the cake slides when you shake the pan.

steps.text: Cut the cake into 4 wedges with the edge of the spatula. Flip each wedge over. If the pan looks dry, add a little more oil around the edges. Cook until the second side is golden and crisp.
steps.tip: Slide the spatula all the way under a wedge before you lift it, and flip it low, close to the pan.

steps.text: Slide the hash browns onto the plate and cover loosely with foil. Cook the other half of the potatoes the same way, with the rest of the oil and butter.
Turn off the stove. Sprinkle the hash browns with a pinch of salt and serve them hot, with ketchup if you like.
